title: How do online retailers make money, and what matters in an e-commerce case?
description: E-commerce economics for case interviews: traffic, conversion, average order value, returns, fulfilment cost and customer acquisition, with a worked funnel…
hook: E-commerce cases test funnel thinking: how many people visit, how many buy, how much they spend, and what each order costs to deliver and, often, to take back.
body:
The funnel

Revenue = visitors × conversion rate × average order value.

A worked example: where to focus

An online store has 1M visitors a month, a 2% conversion rate and £60 average order value: £1.2M a month. Raising conversion to 2.5% adds £300k a month; raising order value to £66 adds £120k. Conversion is the bigger lever here, so start with the checkout and product pages.

The hidden costs

  • Customer acquisition: paid search and social ads.
  • Fulfilment: picking, packing and delivery per order.
  • Returns: in fashion especially, returns can wipe out the profit on many orders.

Typical e-commerce case questions

  • Why have returns costs doubled?
  • Should we offer free delivery?
  • How can we lower customer acquisition cost?
  • Should a store-based retailer grow online?

Find the missing profit in a growing online store

An online retailer gets one million visits a month, converts 2% of visits into orders and has a £60 average order value. Monthly gross orders are 20,000, generating £1.2 million sales before returns. An experiment raises conversion to 2.5%, apparently adding £300,000 of monthly revenue. Whether it improves the business depends on what happens after checkout.

Suppose 20% of orders are returned for full refunds and non-returned orders have a 35% product gross margin. Of the initial £1.2 million, only £960,000 is retained revenue after refunds, producing £336,000 gross product profit before fulfilment, customer acquisition, return shipping and overhead. A paid-marketing campaign could increase sales but destroy value if the extra orders cost too much to acquire or are disproportionately returned.

Separate the funnel into traffic × conversion × basket value, then a contribution bridge: realised sales minus product cost, fulfilment, payment costs, return handling and paid acquisition. Segment new versus repeat customers, organic versus paid traffic, and product categories. A 3% conversion rate in one category is not automatically 'better' than 2% elsewhere if margins and average baskets differ.

A strong hypothesis is specific: 'The conversion decline seems concentrated in mobile checkout after we changed payment options.' Ask for funnel steps by device and week. An answer that begins with 'spend more on SEO' before diagnosing the funnel is unlikely to solve the case.
outro: Next in this topic: How do consumer goods companies make money, and what matters in their cases?
